summary:
Ogun State, a state in southern Nigeria, has no recorded protective statute of its own for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, and the sources reviewed contain no incident series or documented enforcement divergence specific to Ogun. The national framework applies in full, and it criminalises same-sex conduct far beyond marriage.

The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 is the operative national statute. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that the Act also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at the point of entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that religious criminal law in twelve states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers that they face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, 14 years' imprisonment under the 2014 Act, and death-penalty risk in states applying religious criminal law.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

The killing of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama in August 2024 is the most closely documented case of anti-trans violence in this material. Her beaten body was found on a highway in the national capital hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend, and she had expressed fears for her life in the previous year. Nigerian police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. Nothing in this material identifies a comparable Ogun-specific incident series.

Extortion and physical abuse by police officers acting on perceived sexual orientation are recorded nationally. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, on the basis of looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its statutory text, a dynamic that applies in Ogun as it does elsewhere in the country.

Visitors and residents who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Detention conditions for transgender detainees are exposed by the case of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. No sub-national jurisdiction in the sources reviewed departs from that position, and no regional protective law exists for Ogun residents or for travellers passing through the state.
